nodes.name: r-color Ramsey number
nodes.statement: The \(r\)-color Ramsey number \(R_r(k)\) is the minimum \(n\) such that every \(r\)-coloring of the edges of the complete graph \(K_n\) contains a monochromatic clique \(K_k\).
differentia: every \(r\)-coloring of the edges of the complete graph \(K_n\) contains a monochromatic clique \(K_k\)

nodes.name: Erdős–Szekeres bound
nodes.statement: Ramsey~\cite{Ramsey30} proved in 1930 that these numbers are finite, and Erdős and Szekeres~\cite{ESz35} showed in 1935 that \(R_r(k) \le r^{rk}\).
nodes.statement_short: Ramsey numbers are finite (Ramsey) and $R_r(k)\le r^{rk}$ (Erdős–Szekeres).

nodes.name: Exponential improvement for multicolour Ramsey numbers
nodes.statement: \paperref{Theorem 1.1} For each \(r \ge 2\), there exists \(\delta = \delta(r) > 0\) such that \begin{equation*} R_r(k) \le e^{-\delta k} r^{rk} \end{equation*} for all sufficiently large \(k \in \N\).
conclusions: there exists \(\delta = \delta(r) > 0\) such that \begin{equation*} R_r(k) \le e^{-\delta k} r^{rk} \end{equation*} for all sufficiently large \(k \in \N\)
nodes.statement_short: For each $r\ge2$, $R_r(k)\le e^{-\delta k}r^{rk}$ for large $k$: an exponential improvement over Erdős–Szekeres.
nodes.label: thm:Ramsey:multicolour

nodes.name: Multinomial coefficient bound
nodes.statement: \paperref{Lemma A.1} For each \(k,t,r \in \N\) with \(3 \le t \le k\), we have \begin{equation*} \binom{rk-t}{k,\dots,k,k-t} \le e^{-(r-1)t^2/3rk} r^{rk-t}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:multibounds

nodes.name: Proof of multinomial coefficient bound
nodes.statement: To prove this, observe that \begin{equation*} \binom{rk-t}{k,\dots,k,k-t} \binom{rk}{k,\dots,k}^{-1} = \, \prod_{i = 0}^{t - 1} \frac{k - i}{rk - i} = r^{-t} \,\prod_{i = 0}^{t-1} \bigg( 1 - \frac{(r-1)i}{rk - i} \bigg) \le r^{-t} \cdot e^{-(r-1)t^2/3rk}. \end{equation*} Since \(\binom{rk}{k,\dots,k} \le r^{rk}\), the claimed bound follows.
nodes.statement_short: Write the ratio to the balanced multinomial as a product and bound it by an exponential; use $\binom{rk}{k,\dots,k}\le r^{rk}$.

nodes.name: Edge colouring
nodes.statement: An edge colouring of a graph \(G\) with colours \(C\) is a map from the edge set \(E(G)\) to \(C\).
nodes.label: def:edge-colouring

nodes.name: Colour neighbourhood
nodes.statement: Given an edge colouring, we write \(N_i(u)\) to denote the neighbourhood of vertex \(u\) in colour \(i\).
nodes.label: def:colour-neighborhood

nodes.name: Function p_i(X,Y)
nodes.statement: Let \(r, n\in\N\). Given sets \(X,Y \subset V(K_n)\) and a colour \(i \in [r]\), define \begin{equation*} p_i(X,Y) = \min\bigg\{ \frac{|N_i(x) \cap Y|}{|Y|} : x \in X \bigg\}, \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: $p_i(X,Y)$ is the minimum over $x\in X$ of the fraction of $Y$ in the colour-$i$ neighbourhood of $x$.
nodes.label: def:p

nodes.name: cosh√x function
nodes.statement: Define \(\cosh \sqrt{x}\) via its Taylor expansion \begin{equation*} \cosh\sqrt{x} = \sum_{n = 0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{(2n)!}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: def:coshsqrt

nodes.name: Bounds on cosh√x for positive arguments
nodes.statement: \(x \le 2 + \cosh \sqrt{x} \le 3 e^{\sqrt{x}}\) for every \(x > 0\).
nodes.label: lem:coshsqrt-bd-pos

nodes.name: Proof of bounds on cosh√x for positive arguments
nodes.statement: For the lower-bound, using the fact that \(x>0\) and all coefficients of \(\cosh \sqrt{x}\) are positive, \begin{equation*} 2+\cosh \sqrt{x} - x \ge 2 - \frac{x}{2} + \frac{x^2}{24} = \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{24}(x-6)^2 \ge 0. \end{equation*} For the upper bound, we observe that because by comparing coefficients, \begin{equation*} e^{\sqrt{x}} = \sum 3\frac{x^{n/2}}{n!} \ge \cosh\sqrt{x} \end{equation*} Finally, \(2e^{\sqrt{x}}\ge 2\) when \(x>0\).
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound via truncating the Taylor series and completing the square; upper bound by comparing coefficients with $e^{\sqrt{x}}$.

nodes.name: Lower bound
nodes.statement: For the lower-bound, using the fact that \(x>0\) and all coefficients of \(\cosh \sqrt{x}\) are positive, \begin{equation*} 2+\cosh \sqrt{x} - x \ge 2 - \frac{x}{2} + \frac{x^2}{24} = \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{24}(x-6)^2 \ge 0. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Truncate the series and complete the square

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement: For the upper bound, we observe that because by comparing coefficients, \begin{equation*} e^{\sqrt{x}} = \sum 3\frac{x^{n/2}}{n!} \ge \cosh\sqrt{x} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Compare coefficients with $e^{\sqrt{x}}$

nodes.name: Constant term
nodes.statement: Finally, \(2e^{\sqrt{x}}\ge 2\) when \(x>0\).
nodes.statement_short: Absorb the constant 2

nodes.name: Bounds on cosh√x for negative arguments
nodes.statement: \(-1 \le \cosh \sqrt{x} \le 1\) for every \(x < 0\).
nodes.label: lem:coshsqrt-bd-neg

nodes.name: Proof of bounds on cosh√x for negative arguments
nodes.statement: From the Taylor expansion, we get \(\cosh \sqrt{x} = \cos \sqrt{-x}\).
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\cosh\sqrt{x}$ with $\cos\sqrt{-x}$ via the Taylor expansion.

nodes.name: Lower bound for cosh√x
nodes.statement: For all \(x \in \R\), it is \(1 \le 2 + \cosh\sqrt{x}\).
nodes.label: lem:le-coshsqrt

nodes.name: Proof of lower bound for cosh√x
nodes.statement: When \(x\) is negative, we use \(\cosh \sqrt{x} = \cos \sqrt{-x}\ge -1\). When \(x\) is positive this is implied by the fact that all coefficients in the power series of \(\cosh \sqrt{x}\) are positive.
nodes.statement_short: Case on the sign of $x$: cosine bound for negative $x$, positive coefficients for positive $x$.

nodes.name: Special function f
nodes.statement: Let \(r \in \N\). \begin{equation} f(x_1,\dots,x_r) = \sum_{j = 1}^r x_j \prod_{i \ne j} \big( 2 + \cosh\sqrt{x_i} \big). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $f=\sum_j x_j\prod_{i\ne j}(2+\cosh\sqrt{x_i})$.
nodes.label: def:f

nodes.name: Definition of f
nodes.statement: f(x_1,\dots,x_r) = \sum_{j = 1}^r x_j \prod_{i \ne j} \big( 2 + \cosh\sqrt{x_i} \big).
nodes.label: eq:f

nodes.name: Taylor coefficients of f are non-negative
nodes.statement: All of the coefficients of the Taylor expansion of \(f\) are non-negative.
conclusions: All of the coefficients of the Taylor expansion of \(f\) are non-negative.
nodes.label: lem:taylor-nonneg

nodes.name: Proof that Taylor coefficients of f are non-negative
nodes.statement: By definition \(2+\cosh\sqrt{x}\) has positive coefficients. It suffices to observe that the product and sum of two Taylor series with only positive coefficients has again positive coefficients. Since \(f\) is such a combination of sums and products of Taylor series with only positive coefficients, we get the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Sums and products of power series with positive coefficients have positive coefficients.

nodes.name: Positive coefficients of factor
nodes.statement: By definition \(2+\cosh\sqrt{x}\) has positive coefficients.
nodes.statement_short: Each factor $2+\cosh\sqrt{x}$ has positive coefficients

nodes.name: Closure under sum and product
nodes.statement: It suffices to observe that the product and sum of two Taylor series with only positive coefficients has again positive coefficients.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to closure of positive series under sums and products

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since \(f\) is such a combination of sums and products of Taylor series with only positive coefficients, we get the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Apply to $f$

nodes.name: Moments lemma
nodes.statement: \paperref{Lemma 3.2} Let \(U\) and \(U'\) be i.i.d.~random variables taking values in a finite set~\(X\), and let \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r \colon X \to \R^n\) be arbitrary functions. Then \begin{equation*} \Ex\Big[ \big\langle \sigma_1(U),\sigma_1(U') \big\rangle^{\ell_1} \cdots \big\langle \sigma_r(U),\sigma_r(U') \big\rangle^{\ell_r} \Big] \ge 0. \end{equation*} for every \((\ell_1,\dots,\ell_r) \in \Z^r\) with \(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_r \ge 0\).
assumptions: Let \(U\) and \(U'\) be i.i.d.~random variables taking values in a finite set~\(X\)
nodes.statement_short: Mixed moments of the inner products $\langle\sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U')\rangle$ for i.i.d. $U,U'$ are non-negative.
nodes.label: lem:moments

nodes.name: Proof of the moments lemma
nodes.statement: To simplify the notation, let us write \begin{equation*} \big\langle \sigma_1(U),\sigma_1(U') \big\rangle^{\ell_1} \cdots \big\langle \sigma_r(U), \sigma_r(U') \big\rangle^{\ell_r} = \prod_{i = 1}^\ell \big\langle \sigma_{a_i}(U), \sigma_{a_i}(U') \big\rangle \end{equation*} where \(\ell = \ell_1 + \cdots + \ell_r\) and \((a_1,\dots,a_\ell)\) is such that \(\big| \big\{ i \in [\ell] : a_i = j \big\} \big| = \ell_j\) for each \(j \in [r]\). Now set \begin{equation*} Z = \sigma_{a_1}(U) \otimes \sigma_{a_2}(U) \otimes \cdots \otimes \sigma_{a_\ell}(U) \quad \text{and} \quad Z' = \sigma_{a_1}(U') \otimes \sigma_{a_2}(U') \otimes \cdots \otimes \sigma_{a_\ell}(U'), \end{equation*} and note that \begin{equation*} \big\langle Z, Z' \big\rangle = \prod_{i = 1}^\ell \big\langle \sigma_{a_i}(U), \sigma_{a_i}(U') \big\rangle, \end{equation*} since \(\langle u_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes u_r, v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_r \rangle = \langle u_1, v_1 \rangle \cdots \langle v_r , u_r \rangle \) for any vectors \(u_i,v_i \in \R^n\). Finally, note that \(Z\) and \(Z'\) are independent and identically distributed random vectors, and therefore \begin{equation*} \Ex \big[ \langle Z, Z' \rangle \big] = \Ex_{Z'} \big[ \Ex_Z \big[ \langle Z, Z' \rangle \big] \big] = \Ex_{Z'} \big[ \big\langle \Ex[Z], Z' \big\rangle \big] = \big\langle \Ex[Z], \Ex[Z'] \big\rangle \ge 0, \end{equation*} as required, where the final inequality holds because \(\Ex[Z] = \Ex[Z']\).
nodes.statement_short: Tensor the vectors so the product of inner products becomes $\langle Z,Z'\rangle$; independence gives $|\mathbb{E}Z|^2\ge0$.

nodes.name: Rewrite as a product
nodes.statement: To simplify the notation, let us write \begin{equation*} \big\langle \sigma_1(U),\sigma_1(U') \big\rangle^{\ell_1} \cdots \big\langle \sigma_r(U), \sigma_r(U') \big\rangle^{\ell_r} = \prod_{i = 1}^\ell \big\langle \sigma_{a_i}(U), \sigma_{a_i}(U') \big\rangle \end{equation*} where \(\ell = \ell_1 + \cdots + \ell_r\) and \((a_1,\dots,a_\ell)\) is such that \(\big| \big\{ i \in [\ell] : a_i = j \big\} \big| = \ell_j\) for each \(j \in [r]\).
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the monomial as a product of $\ell$ inner products

nodes.name: Tensor vectors
nodes.statement: Now set \begin{equation*} Z = \sigma_{a_1}(U) \otimes \sigma_{a_2}(U) \otimes \cdots \otimes \sigma_{a_\ell}(U) \quad \text{and} \quad Z' = \sigma_{a_1}(U') \otimes \sigma_{a_2}(U') \otimes \cdots \otimes \sigma_{a_\ell}(U'), \end{equation*} and note that \begin{equation*} \big\langle Z, Z' \big\rangle = \prod_{i = 1}^\ell \big\langle \sigma_{a_i}(U), \sigma_{a_i}(U') \big\rangle, \end{equation*} since \(\langle u_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes u_r, v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_r \rangle = \langle u_1, v_1 \rangle \cdots \langle v_r , u_r \rangle \) for any vectors \(u_i,v_i \in \R^n\).
nodes.statement_short: Define tensor products $Z,Z'$ with $\langle Z,Z'\rangle$ the product

nodes.name: Independence
nodes.statement: Finally, note that \(Z\) and \(Z'\) are independent and identically distributed random vectors, and therefore \begin{equation*} \Ex \big[ \langle Z, Z' \rangle \big] = \Ex_{Z'} \big[ \Ex_Z \big[ \langle Z, Z' \rangle \big] \big] = \Ex_{Z'} \big[ \big\langle \Ex[Z], Z' \big\rangle \big] = \big\langle \Ex[Z], \Ex[Z'] \big\rangle \ge 0, \end{equation*} as required, where the final inequality holds because \(\Ex[Z] = \Ex[Z']\).
nodes.statement_short: Independence gives $\langle\mathbb{E}Z,\mathbb{E}Z'\rangle\ge0$

nodes.name: Bounds on cosh(√x)
nodes.statement: Let \(g(x):= cosh(\sqrt{x})\) where \(cosh(x)\) is defined by \(cosh(\sqrt{x})=\overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{x^n}{(2n)!}\), then: \begin{enumerate} \item For all \(x\geq 0\), we have \(x \leq 2+cosh(\sqrt{x}) \leq 3e^{\sqrt{x}}\). \item For all \(x <0\), we have \(-1 \leq cosh(\sqrt{x})\leq 1\). In particular, \(2+cosh(x)\geq 1\) for all \(x\in \mathbb{R}\). \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let \(g(x):= cosh(\sqrt{x})\) where \(cosh(x)\) is defined by \(cosh(\sqrt{x})=\overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{x^n}{(2n)!}\)
nodes.statement_short: For $x\ge0$, $x\le2+\cosh\sqrt{x}\le3e^{\sqrt x}$; for $x<0$, $|\cosh\sqrt x|\le1$, so $2+\cosh\sqrt x\ge1$.

nodes.name: Proof of bounds on cosh(√x)
nodes.statement: To prove (1), let \(x\geq 0\) then: \begin{equation*} 2+cosh(\sqrt{x}) = 3 + \overunderset{\infty}{n=1}{\sum}\frac{x^n}{(2n)!}\geq 3 + \frac{x}{2}+\frac{x^2}{24}. \end{equation*} However, \begin{equation*} 3+\frac{x}{2}+\frac{x^2}{24}\geq x \iff \frac{1}{24}(x^2-12x+72)\geq 0 \iff \frac{1}{24}((x-6)^2+36)\geq 0,s \end{equation*} which concludes the lower bound in the first point. To conclude (1), we note the following for \(x\geq0\): \begin{equation*} 3e^{\sqrt{x}}= 3\overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{x^{n/2}}{n!}\geq 3\overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{x^{n}}{(2n)!} \geq 2 + \overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{x^{n}}{(2n)!}= 2 + cosh(\sqrt{x}). \end{equation*} To prove (2), note that for \(x<0\), \begin{equation*} cosh(\sqrt{x})= \overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{x^n}{(2n)!}= \overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{(-1)^n \sqrt{-x}^{2n}}{(2n)!}= cos(\sqrt{-x}). \end{equation*} (2) then follows by noting that \(cos(\sqrt{-x}) \in [-1,1]\) for all \(x<0\).
nodes.statement_short: Point (1) by truncating the Taylor series and comparing coefficients with $3e^{\sqrt x}$; point (2) by rewriting as $\cos\sqrt{-x}$.

nodes.name: Truncate series
nodes.statement: To prove (1), let \(x\geq 0\) then: \begin{equation*} 2+cosh(\sqrt{x}) = 3 + \overunderset{\infty}{n=1}{\sum}\frac{x^n}{(2n)!}\geq 3 + \frac{x}{2}+\frac{x^2}{24}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $2+\cosh\sqrt x$ below by a quadratic

nodes.name: Quadratic exceeds x
nodes.statement: However, \begin{equation*} 3+\frac{x}{2}+\frac{x^2}{24}\geq x \iff \frac{1}{24}(x^2-12x+72)\geq 0 \iff \frac{1}{24}((x-6)^2+36)\geq 0,s \end{equation*} which concludes the lower bound in the first point.
nodes.statement_short: Complete the square to get the lower bound

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement: To conclude (1), we note the following for \(x\geq0\): \begin{equation*} 3e^{\sqrt{x}}= 3\overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{x^{n/2}}{n!}\geq 3\overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{x^{n}}{(2n)!} \geq 2 + \overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{x^{n}}{(2n)!}= 2 + cosh(\sqrt{x}).
nodes.statement_short: Compare coefficients with $3e^{\sqrt x}$

nodes.name: Cosine identity
nodes.statement: To prove (2), note that for \(x<0\), \begin{equation*} cosh(\sqrt{x})= \overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{x^n}{(2n)!}= \overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{(-1)^n \sqrt{-x}^{2n}}{(2n)!}= cos(\sqrt{-x}).
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $\cosh\sqrt x$ as $\cos\sqrt{-x}$ for $x<0$

nodes.name: Conclude (2)
nodes.statement: (2) then follows by noting that \(cos(\sqrt{-x}) \in [-1,1]\) for all \(x<0\).
nodes.statement_short: Cosine lies in $[-1,1]$

nodes.name: Special function upper bound
nodes.statement: \paperref{Lemma 3.3} Let \(r \in \N\). If \(x_i \ge - 3r\) for all \(i \in [r]\), the function \(f \colon \R^r \to \R\) defined in~\eqref{eq:f} satisfies \begin{equation*} f(x_1,\dots,x_r) \le 3^r r \exp\bigg( \displaystyle\sum_{i = 1}^r \sqrt{ x_i + 3r } \bigg) \end{equation*}
conclusions: the function \(f \colon \R^r \to \R\) defined in~\eqref{eq:f} satisfies \begin{equation*} f(x_1,\dots,x_r) \le 3^r r \exp\bigg( \displaystyle\sum_{i = 1}^r \sqrt{ x_i + 3r } \bigg) \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: If all $x_i\ge-3r$ then $f(x)\le 3^r r\exp(\sum_i\sqrt{x_i+3r})$.
nodes.label: lem:special:function:1

nodes.name: Proof of special function upper bound
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} f(x_1,\dots,x_r)= \Bigl(\overunderset{r}{i=1}{\prod}(2+cosh\sqrt{x_i})\Bigr)\overunderset{r}{j=1}{\sum}\frac{x_j}{2+cosh \sqrt{x_j}} \overset{**}{\leq}r\Bigl(\overunderset{r}{i=1}{\prod} 3e^{\sqrt{x_i+3r}}\Bigr), \end{equation*} To see (**), we write down upper bounds for all the factors of the LHS of (**). First, for every \(i \in [r]\), such that \(x_i \geq 0\), we note that \(cosh(\sqrt{x_i} )\leq cosh(\sqrt{x_i+3r})\) (which follows since all the coefficients in the taylor expansion of \(cosh(\sqrt{y}))\) are non-negative and thus \(cosh(\sqrt{y})\) is non-decreasing on the positive reals. In turn, \(2+cosh(\sqrt{x_i+3r}) \leq 3e^{\sqrt{x_i+3r}}\) by point 1 of the above remark. We conculde that if \(x_i \geq 0\), \(2 + cosh{\sqrt{x_i}} \leq 3 e^{\sqrt{x_i+3r}}\). Next, we condiser the indices \(i \in [r]\) such that \(x_i<0\). In this case \begin{equation*} 2+cosh(\sqrt{x_i})= 2 + cos(\sqrt{-x_i}) \leq 3 \leq 3 e^{\sqrt{x_i+3r}}, \end{equation*} since \(x_i \geq -3r\). It remains to show that \(\frac{x_j}{2+cosh(\sqrt{x_j})} \leq 1\) for every \(j \in [r]\). If \(x_j\geq 0\) this follows directly from point (1) in the above remark. If \(x_j<0\), note that the numerator of the fraction is negative while the denominator is a positive number between 1 and 3 by point(2) of the remark above.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $f$ as a product times $\sum_j x_j/(2+\cosh\sqrt{x_j})$ and bound each factor, splitting on the sign of $x_i$.

nodes.name: Factor f
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} f(x_1,\dots,x_r)= \Bigl(\overunderset{r}{i=1}{\prod}(2+cosh\sqrt{x_i})\Bigr)\overunderset{r}{j=1}{\sum}\frac{x_j}{2+cosh \sqrt{x_j}} \overset{**}{\leq}r\Bigl(\overunderset{r}{i=1}{\prod} 3e^{\sqrt{x_i+3r}}\Bigr), \end{equation*} To see (**), we write down upper bounds for all the factors of the LHS of (**).
nodes.statement_short: Factor $f$ and state the inequality (**) to prove

nodes.name: Case x_i ≥ 0
nodes.statement: First, for every \(i \in [r]\), such that \(x_i \geq 0\), we note that \(cosh(\sqrt{x_i} )\leq cosh(\sqrt{x_i+3r})\) (which follows since all the coefficients in the taylor expansion of \(cosh(\sqrt{y}))\) are non-negative and thus \(cosh(\sqrt{y})\) is non-decreasing on the positive reals. In turn, \(2+cosh(\sqrt{x_i+3r}) \leq 3e^{\sqrt{x_i+3r}}\) by point 1 of the above remark. We conculde that if \(x_i \geq 0\), \(2 + cosh{\sqrt{x_i}} \leq 3 e^{\sqrt{x_i+3r}}\).
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity and point 1 of the remark bound the factor

nodes.name: Case x_i < 0
nodes.statement: Next, we condiser the indices \(i \in [r]\) such that \(x_i<0\). In this case \begin{equation*} 2+cosh(\sqrt{x_i})= 2 + cos(\sqrt{-x_i}) \leq 3 \leq 3 e^{\sqrt{x_i+3r}}, \end{equation*} since \(x_i \geq -3r\).
nodes.statement_short: Cosine bound gives factor at most 3

nodes.name: Bound the sum
nodes.statement: It remains to show that \(\frac{x_j}{2+cosh(\sqrt{x_j})} \leq 1\) for every \(j \in [r]\). If \(x_j\geq 0\) this follows directly from point (1) in the above remark. If \(x_j<0\), note that the numerator of the fraction is negative while the denominator is a positive number between 1 and 3 by point(2) of the remark above.
nodes.statement_short: Each ratio $x_j/(2+\cosh\sqrt{x_j})$ is at most 1

nodes.name: Special function lower bound
nodes.statement: \paperref{Lemma 3.3} Let \(r \in \N\). If there exists an \(i \in [r]\) with \(x_i \le - 3r\), the function \(f \colon \R^r \to \R\) defined in~\eqref{eq:f} satisfies \begin{equation*} f(x_1,\dots,x_r) \le -1 \end{equation*}
conclusions: the function \(f \colon \R^r \to \R\) defined in~\eqref{eq:f} satisfies \begin{equation*} f(x_1,\dots,x_r) \le -1 \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: If some $x_i\le-3r$ then $f(x)\le-1$.
nodes.label: lem:special:function:2

nodes.name: Proof of special function lower bound
nodes.statement: Let \(i \in [r]\) satisfy \(x_i \leq -3r\). Note that if \(x\geq 0\), then \(\frac{x}{2+cosh(\sqrt{x})}\leq 1\) by point (1) of the above remark. Trivially, we have \(\frac{x}{2+cosh{\sqrt{x}}}<0\leq 1\) for \(x<0\) (note that \(2+cosh(\sqrt{x})\geq 1\).) Therefore, we have \begin{equation*} \underset{j \in [r], j \neq i}{\sum} \frac{x_j}{2+cosh(\sqrt{x_j})} \leq r-1. \end{equation*} On the other hand, we know that \(\frac{x_i}{2+cosh(\sqrt{x_i})} \leq \frac{x_i}{3}\) by part (2) in the remark above and therefore, \begin{equation*} \overunderset{r}{j=1}{\sum}\frac{x_j}{2+cosh(\sqrt{x_j})}\leq \frac{x_i}{3}+r-1\leq -1. \end{equation*} Finally we write \begin{equation*} f(x_1,\dots,x_r) = \Bigl(\overunderset{r}{i=1}{\prod}(2+cosh\sqrt{x_i})\Bigr)\overunderset{r}{j=1}{\sum}\frac{x_j}{2+cosh \sqrt{x_j}} \leq -1, \end{equation*} since the sum in the last term is \(\leq -1\) while the product is at least \(1\) (each factor in the product is at least 1).
nodes.statement_short: Bound each ratio $x_j/(2+\cosh\sqrt{x_j})$ by 1 and the $i$-th by $x_i/3$, so the sum is $\le-1$; the product is $\ge1$.

nodes.name: Fix bad index
nodes.statement: Let \(i \in [r]\) satisfy \(x_i \leq -3r\). Note that if \(x\geq 0\), then \(\frac{x}{2+cosh(\sqrt{x})}\leq 1\) by point (1) of the above remark. Trivially, we have \(\frac{x}{2+cosh{\sqrt{x}}}<0\leq 1\) for \(x<0\) (note that \(2+cosh(\sqrt{x})\geq 1\).)
nodes.statement_short: Fix $i$ with $x_i\le-3r$; each ratio is at most 1

nodes.name: Sum over j ≠ i
nodes.statement: Therefore, we have \begin{equation*} \underset{j \in [r], j \neq i}{\sum} \frac{x_j}{2+cosh(\sqrt{x_j})} \leq r-1. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Other ratios sum to at most $r-1$

nodes.name: Bound i-th ratio
nodes.statement: On the other hand, we know that \(\frac{x_i}{2+cosh(\sqrt{x_i})} \leq \frac{x_i}{3}\) by part (2) in the remark above and therefore, \begin{equation*} \overunderset{r}{j=1}{\sum}\frac{x_j}{2+cosh(\sqrt{x_j})}\leq \frac{x_i}{3}+r-1\leq -1. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: The $i$-th ratio is at most $x_i/3$, so the sum is $\le-1$

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Finally we write \begin{equation*} f(x_1,\dots,x_r) = \Bigl(\overunderset{r}{i=1}{\prod}(2+cosh\sqrt{x_i})\Bigr)\overunderset{r}{j=1}{\sum}\frac{x_j}{2+cosh \sqrt{x_j}} \leq -1, \end{equation*} since the sum in the last term is \(\leq -1\) while the product is at least \(1\) (each factor in the product is at least 1).
nodes.statement_short: Product $\ge1$ times sum $\le-1$

nodes.name: Key idea of the special function bounds
nodes.statement: The key idea in the two lemmas above was to find an entire function, \(2 + \cosh\sqrt{x}\), which \((a)\) has a Taylor expansion at \(x = 0\) with non-negative coefficients; \((b)\) is bounded on the negative real axis; and \((c)\) does not grow too quickly on the positive axis. The Phragm\'en--Lindel\"of theorem implies that functions satisfying \((a)\) and \((b)\) must grow at least as fast as \(\exp\big( \Omega(\sqrt{x}) \big)\) on the positive real axis. Thus the bound on the growth of \(f\) given by the lemma is essentially best possible for constructions of this type.
nodes.statement_short: $2+\cosh\sqrt x$ has non-negative Taylor coefficients, is bounded on the negative axis and grows slowly; Phragmén–Lindelöf shows this growth is optimal.

nodes.name: Geometric lemma
nodes.statement: \paperref{Lemma 3.1} Let \(r, n\in\N\). Set \(\beta = 3^{-4r}\) and \(C = 4r^{3/2}\). Let \(U\) and \(U'\) be i.i.d.~random variables taking values in a finite set~\(X\), and let \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r \colon X \to \R^n\) be arbitrary functions. There exists \(\lambda\ge-1\) and \(i\in[r]\) such that \begin{equation*} \Pr\Big( \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \ge \lambda \, \text{ and } \, \big\langle \sigma_j(U), \sigma_j(U') \big\rangle \ge -1 \, \text{ for all } \, j \ne i \Big) \ge \beta e^{- C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}}. \end{equation*}
assumptions: Let \(U\) and \(U'\) be i.i.d.~random variables taking values in a finite set~\(X\)
conclusions: There exists \(\lambda\ge-1\) and \(i\in[r]\) such that \begin{equation*} \Pr\Big( \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \ge \lambda \, \text{ and } \, \big\langle \sigma_j(U), \sigma_j(U') \big\rangle \ge -1 \, \text{ for all } \, j \ne i \Big) \ge \beta e^{- C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: For i.i.d. $U,U'$ and maps $\sigma_i$, some colour $i$ and $\lambda\ge-1$ have $\langle\sigma_i\rangle\ge\lambda$ and all others $\ge-1$ with probability $\ge\beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda+1}}$.
nodes.label: lem:geometric

nodes.name: Proof of the geometric lemma
nodes.statement: For each \(i \in [r]\), define \(Z_i = 3r\big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle\), and let \(E\) be the event that \(Z_i \ge -3r\) for every \(i \in [r]\). Consider two cases: First assume \(\Pr(E) \ge \beta\). Note that \begin{equation*} \Pr(E) = \Pr\Big( Z_i \ge - 3r \, \text{ for all } \, i \in [r] \Big), \end{equation*} so with \(\lambda = -1\), \begin{align*} \beta e^{-C\times 0} &= \beta\\ &\le \Pr(E)\\ &= \Pr\Big(3r\big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \ge -3r \text{ for all }i\Big)\\ &= \Pr\Big( \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \ge \lambda \, \text{ and } \, \big\langle \sigma_j(U), \sigma_j(U') \big\rangle \ge -1 \, \text{ for all } \, j \ne i \Big) \end{align*} hence the claimed inequality holds. Now, assume \(\Pr(E) \le \beta\) and assume for the sake of a contradiction that for all \(\lambda \geq -1\), \begin{align} \Pr\left(E \cap \left( \bigcup_{i \in [r]} \left\{ \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \ge \lambda \right\}\right)\right) < \beta r e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}}. \end{align} Observe that, since \(x \le 2 + \cosh\sqrt{x}\) (\autoref{lem:le-coshsqrt}) and using \autoref{lem:moments} and linearity of expectation, \[ \Ex\big[ f\big( Z_1,\ldots,Z_r \big) \big] \ge 0 \] We hence have \begin{align*} 0 &\le \Ex\big[ f\big( Z_1,\ldots,Z_r \big) \big]\\ &= \Ex\big[ f\big( Z_1,\ldots,Z_r \big) \mathbf{1}_E \big] + \Ex\big[ f\big( Z_1,\ldots,Z_r \big) \mathbf{1}_{E^c} \big]\\ &\le \Ex\left[ 3^r r \exp\bigg( \displaystyle\sum_{i = 1}^r \sqrt{ Z_i + 3r } \bigg) \mathbf{1}_E \right] + \Ex\big[-1 \cdot \mathbf{1}_{E^c} \big] \end{align*} where we use \autoref{lem:special:function:1} to bound the case for \(E\), and \autoref{lem:special:function:2} for \(E^c\). It follows that \begin{equation} 1 - \Pr(E) \le 3^r r \cdot \Ex\bigg[ \exp\bigg( \sum_{i = 1}^r \sqrt{ Z_i + 3r } \bigg) \mathbf{1}_E \bigg]. \end{equation} Let \(M = \max \big\{ \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle : i \in [r] \big\}\). For any constant \(c \le C - 1\), we have \begin{align} \exp(c\sqrt{M+1})\id_E&= \id_E \Bigl(e^{c\sqrt{1-1}}+ \int_{-1}^M \frac{ce^{c\sqrt{\lambda+1}}}{2\sqrt{\lambda+1}} d\lambda\Bigr)\\ &= \id_E+ \int_{-1}^{\infty} \id_{E,\{M\geq \lambda\}}\frac{ce^{c\sqrt{\lambda+1}}}{2\sqrt{\lambda+1}} d\lambda. \end{align} Given any \(c \leq C-1\) we take the expected value of both sides of the previous equation and apply Tonelli's theorem to obtain: \begin{align*} \Ex\Big[ \exp\big( c \sqrt{M + 1} \big) \mathbf{1}_E \Big] & \\ & \le \, \Pr(E) + \int_{-1}^\infty \Pr\Big( \big\{ M \ge \lambda \big\} \cap E \Big) \cdot \frac{c}{2\sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \cdot e^{c \sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \,\mathrm{d}\lambda\\ & \le \, \beta + \int_{-1}^\infty \frac{\beta r c}{2\sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \cdot e^{- C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}+c\sqrt{\lambda+1}} \,\mathrm{d}\lambda\\ & \le \, \beta + \beta r \int_{-1}^\infty \frac{c}{2\sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \cdot e^{- \sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \,\mathrm{d}\lambda\\ & \le \, \beta (cr + 1), \end{align*} where in the second inequality we used (\autoref{eq:max:big:and:E:no}) and \(\Pr(E) \le \beta\); in the third we used \(c \le C - 1\); and in the last inequality we used the fact that \(\int_0^\infty \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} e^{-\sqrt{x}} \, \mathrm{d}x = 1\). Note that the second and third inequalities rely on the non-negativity of the integrand. In particular, applying this with \(c = \sqrt{3}r^{3/2}\), and recalling that \(C = 4r^{3/2} \ge c + 1\) and \(\beta = 3^{-4r}\), it follows that \begin{align} 1 - \Pr(E) &\le 3^r r \cdot \Ex\bigg[ \exp\bigg( \sum_{i = 1}^r \sqrt{ Z_i + 3r } \bigg) \mathbf{1}_E \bigg]\\ &\le 3^r r \cdot \Ex\bigg[ \exp\bigg( r \cdot \max_{i \in [r]} \sqrt{ Z_i + 3r } \bigg) \mathbf{1}_E \bigg]\\ &= 3^r r \cdot \Ex\bigg[ \exp\bigg( r \cdot \sqrt{ 3r} \cdot \sqrt{ (M + 1) } \bigg) \mathbf{1}_E \bigg]\\ &\le 3^r r \cdot \beta (r^{2}\sqrt{3r} + 1) \le 1/3, \end{align} which contradicts our assumption that \(\Pr(E) \le \beta\). Hence, there exists \(\lambda \ge -1\) such that \begin{align} \beta r e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}} &\le \Pr\left(E \cap \left( \bigcup_{i \in [r]} \left\{ \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \ge \lambda \right\}\right) \right) \\ &\le \sum_{i \in [r]} \Pr\left(E \cap \left\{ \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \ge \lambda \right\} \right)\\ &\le r \cdot \max_{i \in [r]} \Pr\left(E \cap \left\{ \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \ge \lambda \right\} \right) , \end{align} and therefore there exists an \(i \in [r]\) as required.
nodes.statement_short: Two cases on $\Pr(E)$; in the second, contradiction via $\mathbb{E}f(Z)\ge0$ (moments lemma) against the special-function bounds. The key step integrates tail bounds for $\exp(c\sqrt{M+1})$ with Tonelli.

nodes.name: Assume small tail
nodes.statement: Now, assume \(\Pr(E) \le \beta\) and assume for the sake of a contradiction that for all \(\lambda \geq -1\), \begin{align} \Pr\left(E \cap \left( \bigcup_{i \in [r]} \left\{ \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \ge \lambda \right\}\right)\right) < \beta r e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Assume the tail bound fails for all $\lambda$

nodes.name: Expectation of f non-negative
nodes.statement: Observe that, since \(x \le 2 + \cosh\sqrt{x}\) (\autoref{lem:le-coshsqrt}) and using \autoref{lem:moments} and linearity of expectation, \[ \Ex\big[ f\big( Z_1,\ldots,Z_r \big) \big] \ge 0 \]
nodes.statement_short: Moments lemma gives $\mathbb{E}f(Z)\ge0$

nodes.name: Split on E
nodes.statement: We hence have \begin{align*} 0 &\le \Ex\big[ f\big( Z_1,\ldots,Z_r \big) \big]\\ &= \Ex\big[ f\big( Z_1,\ldots,Z_r \big) \mathbf{1}_E \big] + \Ex\big[ f\big( Z_1,\ldots,Z_r \big) \mathbf{1}_{E^c} \big]\\ &\le \Ex\left[ 3^r r \exp\bigg( \displaystyle\sum_{i = 1}^r \sqrt{ Z_i + 3r } \bigg) \mathbf{1}_E \right] + \Ex\big[-1 \cdot \mathbf{1}_{E^c} \big] \end{align*} where we use \autoref{lem:special:function:1} to bound the case for \(E\), and \autoref{lem:special:function:2} for \(E^c\). It follows that \begin{equation} 1 - \Pr(E) \le 3^r r \cdot \Ex\bigg[ \exp\bigg( \sum_{i = 1}^r \sqrt{ Z_i + 3r } \bigg) \mathbf{1}_E \bigg]. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Introduce M
nodes.statement: Let \(M = \max \big\{ \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle : i \in [r] \big\}\). For any constant \(c \le C - 1\), we have \begin{align} \exp(c\sqrt{M+1})\id_E&= \id_E \Bigl(e^{c\sqrt{1-1}}+ \int_{-1}^M \frac{ce^{c\sqrt{\lambda+1}}}{2\sqrt{\lambda+1}} d\lambda\Bigr)\\ &= \id_E+ \int_{-1}^{\infty} \id_{E,\{M\geq \lambda\}}\frac{ce^{c\sqrt{\lambda+1}}}{2\sqrt{\lambda+1}} d\lambda. \end{align}

nodes.statement: Given any \(c \leq C-1\) we take the expected value of both sides of the previous equation and apply Tonelli's theorem to obtain: \begin{align*} \Ex\Big[ \exp\big( c \sqrt{M + 1} \big) \mathbf{1}_E \Big] & \\ & \le \, \Pr(E) + \int_{-1}^\infty \Pr\Big( \big\{ M \ge \lambda \big\} \cap E \Big) \cdot \frac{c}{2\sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \cdot e^{c \sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \,\mathrm{d}\lambda\\ & \le \, \beta + \int_{-1}^\infty \frac{\beta r c}{2\sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \cdot e^{- C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}+c\sqrt{\lambda+1}} \,\mathrm{d}\lambda\\ & \le \, \beta + \beta r \int_{-1}^\infty \frac{c}{2\sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \cdot e^{- \sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \,\mathrm{d}\lambda\\ & \le \, \beta (cr + 1), \end{align*} where in the second inequality we used (\autoref{eq:max:big:and:E:no}) and \(\Pr(E) \le \beta\); in the third we used \(c \le C - 1\); and in the last inequality we used the fact that \(\int_0^\infty \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} e^{-\sqrt{x}} \, \mathrm{d}x = 1\). Note that the second and third inequalities rely on the non-negativity of the integrand.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the tail bound to get $\le\beta(cr+1)$

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: In particular, applying this with \(c = \sqrt{3}r^{3/2}\), and recalling that \(C = 4r^{3/2} \ge c + 1\) and \(\beta = 3^{-4r}\), it follows that \begin{align} 1 - \Pr(E) &\le 3^r r \cdot \Ex\bigg[ \exp\bigg( \sum_{i = 1}^r \sqrt{ Z_i + 3r } \bigg) \mathbf{1}_E \bigg]\\ &\le 3^r r \cdot \Ex\bigg[ \exp\bigg( r \cdot \max_{i \in [r]} \sqrt{ Z_i + 3r } \bigg) \mathbf{1}_E \bigg]\\ &= 3^r r \cdot \Ex\bigg[ \exp\bigg( r \cdot \sqrt{ 3r} \cdot \sqrt{ (M + 1) } \bigg) \mathbf{1}_E \bigg]\\ &\le 3^r r \cdot \beta (r^{2}\sqrt{3r} + 1) \le 1/3, \end{align} which contradicts our assumption that \(\Pr(E) \le \beta\).
nodes.statement_short: Choose $c$ to get $1-\Pr(E)\le1/3$

nodes.name: Pigeonhole colour
nodes.statement: Hence, there exists \(\lambda \ge -1\) such that \begin{align} \beta r e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}} &\le \Pr\left(E \cap \left( \bigcup_{i \in [r]} \left\{ \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \ge \lambda \right\}\right) \right) \\ &\le \sum_{i \in [r]} \Pr\left(E \cap \left\{ \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \ge \lambda \right\} \right)\\ &\le r \cdot \max_{i \in [r]} \Pr\left(E \cap \left\{ \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \ge \lambda \right\} \right) , \end{align} and therefore there exists an \(i \in [r]\) as required.
nodes.statement_short: Union bound gives a colour $i$

nodes.name: Key lemma
nodes.statement: \paperref{Lemma 2.2} Let \(r, n\in\N\). Set \(\beta = 3^{-4r}\) and \(C = 4r^{3/2}\). Let \(\chi\) be an \(r\)-colouring of \(E(K_n)\), let \(X,Y_1,\ldots,Y_r \subset V(K_n)\) be non-empty sets of vertices, and let \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r > 0\). There exists a vertex \(x \in X\), a colour \(\ell \in [r]\), sets \(X' \subset X\) and \(Y'_1,\ldots,Y'_r\,\) with \(Y'_i \subset N_i(x) \cap Y_i\,\) for each \(i \in [r]\), and \(\lambda \ge -1\), such that \begin{equation} \beta e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda + 1}} |X| \le |X'| \qquad \text{and} \qquad p_\ell(X,Y_\ell) + \lambda \alpha_\ell \le p_\ell( X', Y'_\ell ) , \end{equation} and moreover \begin{equation} |Y'_i| = p_i(X,Y_i) |Y_i| \qquad \text{and} \qquad p_i(X,Y_i) - \alpha_i \le p_i( X', Y'_i ) \end{equation} for every \(i \in [r]\).
assumptions: let \(X,Y_1,\ldots,Y_r \subset V(K_n)\) be non-empty sets of vertices
conclusions: There exists a vertex \(x \in X\), a colour \(\ell \in [r]\), sets \(X' \subset X\) and \(Y'_1,\ldots,Y'_r\,\) with \(Y'_i \subset N_i(x) \cap Y_i\,\) for each \(i \in [r]\), and \(\lambda \ge -1\), such that \begin{equation} \beta e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda + 1}} |X| \le |X'| \qquad \text{and} \qquad p_\ell(X,Y_\ell) + \lambda \alpha_\ell \le p_\ell( X', Y'_\ell ) , \end{equation} and moreover \begin{equation} |Y'_i| = p_i(X,Y_i) |Y_i| \qquad \text{and} \qquad p_i(X,Y_i) - \alpha_i \le p_i( X', Y'_i ) \end{equation} for every \(i \in [r]\).
nodes.statement_short: Find $x$, colour $\ell$, $X'\subset X$ and $Y_i'\subset N_i(x)\cap Y_i$ with $|X'|\ge\beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda+1}}|X|$, density boosted by $\lambda\alpha_\ell$ in colour $\ell$ and lost by at most $\alpha_i$ elsewhere.
nodes.label: lem:key-lemma

nodes.name: Proof of the key lemma
nodes.statement: For each colour \(i \in [r]\), define a function \(\sigma_i \colon X \to \R^{\cup_i Y_i}\) as follows: for each \(x \in X\), choose a set \(N'_i(x) \subset N_i(x) \cap Y_i\) of size exactly \(p_i|Y_i|\), where \(p_i = p_i(X,Y_i)\), and set \begin{equation*} \sigma_i(x) = \frac{\id_{N'_i(x)} - p_i\id_{Y_i}}{\sqrt{\alpha_ip_i|Y_i|}}, \end{equation*} where \(\id_S \in \{0,1\}^{\cup_i Y_i}\) denotes the indicator function of the set \(S\). Note that, for any \(x,y\in X\), \begin{equation*} \lambda \le \big\langle \sigma_i(x),\sigma_i(y) \big\rangle \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \big( p_i + \lambda\alpha_i \big) p_i |Y_i| \le |N'_i(x) \cap N'_i(y)|. \end{equation*} Indeed, for every \(x,y\in X\), we have \begin{multline} \begin{aligned} \alpha_ip_i|Y_i| \langle \sigma_i(x),\sigma_i(y) \rangle &= \langle \id_{N'_i(x)}- p_i\id_{Y_i},\id_{N'_i(y)}- p_i\id_{Y_i}\rangle\\ &= \Bigl(\big\langle \id_{N'_i(x)},\id_{N'_i(y)}\big\rangle +p_i^2\langle \id_{Y_i}, \id_{Y_i}\rangle - p_i \langle \id_{N'_i(x)},\id_{Y_i}\rangle- p_i \langle \id_{N'_i(y)},\id_{Y_i}\rangle\Bigr)\\ &= \Bigl(|N'_i(x) \cap N'_i(y)|-p_i^2|Y_i| \Bigr), \end{aligned} \end{multline} Where the last ineqaulity follows since \(|N'_i(x)|= N'_i(y)|= p_i|Y_i|\) and both sets are subsets of \(Y_i\). Now, by \autoref{lem:geometric}, there exists \(\lambda \ge -1\) and colour \(\ell \in [r]\) such that \begin{equation} \beta e^{- C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \le \Pr\Big( \lambda \le \big\langle \sigma_\ell(U),\sigma_\ell(U') \big\rangle \, \text{ and } \, -1 \le \big\langle \sigma_i(U), \sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \, \text{ for all } \, i \ne \ell \Big) . \end{equation} where \(U\), \(U'\) are independent random variables distributed uniformly in the set~\(X\). We claim that there exists a vertex \(x \in X\) and a set \(X' \subset X\) such that, \begin{equation*} \beta e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda + 1}} |X| \le |X'| \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} \big( p_\ell + \lambda\alpha_\ell \big) p_\ell |Y_\ell | \le |N'_\ell(x) \cap N'_\ell(y)| \end{equation*} for every \(y \in X'\), and \begin{equation*} \big( p_i - \alpha_i \big) p_i |Y_i| \le |N'_i(x) \cap N'_i(y)| \end{equation*} for every \(y \in X'\) and \(i \in [r]\). To see this, we let \begin{equation*} P= \Biggl\{(x,x'): x,x' \in X , \lambda \le \big\langle \sigma_\ell(x),\sigma_\ell(x') \big\rangle \, \text{ and } \, -1 \le \big\langle \sigma_i(x), \sigma_i(x') \big\rangle \, \text{ for all } \, i \ne \ell \Biggr\}. \end{equation*} Since \(U\) and \(U'\) are independent and uniformly distributed over \(x\), Equation \autoref{eq: geometric-app} implies that \begin{equation} |P|\geq \beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}}|X|^2. \end{equation} However, by averaging, there must then exist a vertex \(x \in X\) such that: \begin{equation} |X'|:=\bigl|\{y: (x,y) \in P \} \bigr| \ge \frac{\beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda+1}}|X|^2}{|X|}\geq \beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda+1}}|X|. \end{equation} We can them simply pick this \(X'\) to be the desired subset. Setting \(Y'_i = N'_i(x)\) for each \(i \in [r]\), it follows that \begin{multline} \begin{aligned} p_\ell(X,Y_\ell) + \lambda \alpha_\ell &= \frac{ \big( p_\ell + \lambda\alpha_\ell \big) p_\ell |Y_\ell |}{p_\ell |Y_\ell|}\\ &= \frac{ \big( p_\ell + \lambda\alpha_\ell \big) p_\ell |Y_\ell |}{| N'_\ell (x)|}\\ &= \min\bigg\{ \frac{ \big( p_\ell + \lambda\alpha_\ell \big) p_\ell |Y_\ell |}{| N'_\ell (x)|} : x' \in X' \bigg\}\\ &\le \min\bigg\{ \frac{|N'_\ell(x') \cap N'_\ell (x)|}{| N'_\ell (x)|} : x' \in X' \bigg\}\\ &= \min\bigg\{ \frac{|N_\ell(x') \cap N'_\ell (x)|}{| N'_\ell (x)|} : x' \in X' \bigg\}\\ &= p_\ell\big( X', N'_\ell (x) \big) = p_\ell\big( X', Y'_\ell \big) \\ \end{aligned} \end{multline} and \begin{equation*} p_i(X,Y_i) - \alpha_i \le \qquad p_i\big( X', Y'_i \big) \end{equation*} for every \(i \in [r]\), as required.
nodes.statement_short: Encode neighbourhoods as normalized vectors $\sigma_i(x)$ and apply the geometric lemma; then average to find $x$ and $X'$.

nodes.name: Define σ_i
nodes.statement: For each colour \(i \in [r]\), define a function \(\sigma_i \colon X \to \R^{\cup_i Y_i}\) as follows: for each \(x \in X\), choose a set \(N'_i(x) \subset N_i(x) \cap Y_i\) of size exactly \(p_i|Y_i|\), where \(p_i = p_i(X,Y_i)\), and set \begin{equation*} \sigma_i(x) = \frac{\id_{N'_i(x)} - p_i\id_{Y_i}}{\sqrt{\alpha_ip_i|Y_i|}}, \end{equation*} where \(\id_S \in \{0,1\}^{\cup_i Y_i}\) denotes the indicator function of the set \(S\).
nodes.statement_short: Encode trimmed neighbourhoods as vectors $\sigma_i(x)$

nodes.name: Inner product identity
nodes.statement: Note that, for any \(x,y\in X\), \begin{equation*} \lambda \le \big\langle \sigma_i(x),\sigma_i(y) \big\rangle \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \big( p_i + \lambda\alpha_i \big) p_i |Y_i| \le |N'_i(x) \cap N'_i(y)|. \end{equation*} Indeed, for every \(x,y\in X\), we have \begin{multline} \begin{aligned} \alpha_ip_i|Y_i| \langle \sigma_i(x),\sigma_i(y) \rangle &= \langle \id_{N'_i(x)}- p_i\id_{Y_i},\id_{N'_i(y)}- p_i\id_{Y_i}\rangle\\ &= \Bigl(\big\langle \id_{N'_i(x)},\id_{N'_i(y)}\big\rangle +p_i^2\langle \id_{Y_i}, \id_{Y_i}\rangle - p_i \langle \id_{N'_i(x)},\id_{Y_i}\rangle- p_i \langle \id_{N'_i(y)},\id_{Y_i}\rangle\Bigr)\\ &= \Bigl(|N'_i(x) \cap N'_i(y)|-p_i^2|Y_i| \Bigr), \end{aligned} \end{multline} Where the last ineqaulity follows since \(|N'_i(x)|= N'_i(y)|= p_i|Y_i|\) and both sets are subsets of \(Y_i\).
nodes.statement_short: Inner products measure common-neighbourhood sizes

nodes.name: Apply geometric lemma
nodes.statement: Now, by \autoref{lem:geometric}, there exists \(\lambda \ge -1\) and colour \(\ell \in [r]\) such that \begin{equation} \beta e^{- C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \le \Pr\Big( \lambda \le \big\langle \sigma_\ell(U),\sigma_\ell(U') \big\rangle \, \text{ and } \, -1 \le \big\langle \sigma_i(U), \sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \, \text{ for all } \, i \ne \ell \Big) . \end{equation} where \(U\), \(U'\) are independent random variables distributed uniformly in the set~\(X\).
nodes.statement_short: Get $\lambda$ and colour $\ell$ from the geometric lemma

nodes.name: Claim: x and X'
nodes.statement: We claim that there exists a vertex \(x \in X\) and a set \(X' \subset X\) such that, \begin{equation*} \beta e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda + 1}} |X| \le |X'| \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} \big( p_\ell + \lambda\alpha_\ell \big) p_\ell |Y_\ell | \le |N'_\ell(x) \cap N'_\ell(y)| \end{equation*} for every \(y \in X'\), and \begin{equation*} \big( p_i - \alpha_i \big) p_i |Y_i| \le |N'_i(x) \cap N'_i(y)| \end{equation*} for every \(y \in X'\) and \(i \in [r]\). To see this, we let \begin{equation*} P= \Biggl\{(x,x'): x,x' \in X , \lambda \le \big\langle \sigma_\ell(x),\sigma_\ell(x') \big\rangle \, \text{ and } \, -1 \le \big\langle \sigma_i(x), \sigma_i(x') \big\rangle \, \text{ for all } \, i \ne \ell \Biggr\}. \end{equation*} Since \(U\) and \(U'\) are independent and uniformly distributed over \(x\), Equation \autoref{eq: geometric-app} implies that \begin{equation} |P|\geq \beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}}|X|^2. \end{equation} However, by averaging, there must then exist a vertex \(x \in X\) such that: \begin{equation} |X'|:=\bigl|\{y: (x,y) \in P \} \bigr| \ge \frac{\beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda+1}}|X|^2}{|X|}\geq \beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda+1}}|X|. \end{equation} We can them simply pick this \(X'\) to be the desired subset.
nodes.statement_short: Claim there are $x$ and large $X'$ with good common neighbourhoods

nodes.name: Define P
nodes.statement: To see this, we let \begin{equation*} P= \Biggl\{(x,x'): x,x' \in X , \lambda \le \big\langle \sigma_\ell(x),\sigma_\ell(x') \big\rangle \, \text{ and } \, -1 \le \big\langle \sigma_i(x), \sigma_i(x') \big\rangle \, \text{ for all } \, i \ne \ell \Biggr\}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Set of good pairs

nodes.name: Count pairs
nodes.statement: Since \(U\) and \(U'\) are independent and uniformly distributed over \(x\), Equation \autoref{eq: geometric-app} implies that \begin{equation} |P|\geq \beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}}|X|^2. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $|P|\ge\beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda+1}}|X|^2$

nodes.name: Averaging
nodes.statement: However, by averaging, there must then exist a vertex \(x \in X\) such that: \begin{equation} |X'|:=\bigl|\{y: (x,y) \in P \} \bigr| \ge \frac{\beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda+1}}|X|^2}{|X|}\geq \beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda+1}}|X|. \end{equation} We can them simply pick this \(X'\) to be the desired subset.
nodes.statement_short: Some $x$ has many partners

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Setting \(Y'_i = N'_i(x)\) for each \(i \in [r]\), it follows that \begin{multline} \begin{aligned} p_\ell(X,Y_\ell) + \lambda \alpha_\ell &= \frac{ \big( p_\ell + \lambda\alpha_\ell \big) p_\ell |Y_\ell |}{p_\ell |Y_\ell|}\\ &= \frac{ \big( p_\ell + \lambda\alpha_\ell \big) p_\ell |Y_\ell |}{| N'_\ell (x)|}\\ &= \min\bigg\{ \frac{ \big( p_\ell + \lambda\alpha_\ell \big) p_\ell |Y_\ell |}{| N'_\ell (x)|} : x' \in X' \bigg\}\\ &\le \min\bigg\{ \frac{|N'_\ell(x') \cap N'_\ell (x)|}{| N'_\ell (x)|} : x' \in X' \bigg\}\\ &= \min\bigg\{ \frac{|N_\ell(x') \cap N'_\ell (x)|}{| N'_\ell (x)|} : x' \in X' \bigg\}\\ &= p_\ell\big( X', N'_\ell (x) \big) = p_\ell\big( X', Y'_\ell \big) \\ \end{aligned} \end{multline} and \begin{equation*} p_i(X,Y_i) - \alpha_i \le \qquad p_i\big( X', Y'_i \big) \end{equation*} for every \(i \in [r]\), as required.
nodes.statement_short: Set $Y_i'=N_i'(x)$ and verify the density bounds

nodes.name: Multicolour Book Algorithm
nodes.statement: Set \(T_1 = \cdots = T_r = \emptyset\), and repeat the following steps until either \(X = \emptyset\) or \(\max\big\{ |T_i| : i \in [r] \big\} = t\). \begin{enumerate} \item Applying the key lemma: let the vertex \(x \in X\), the colour \(\ell \in [r]\), the sets \(X' \subset X\) and \(Y'_1,\ldots,Y'_r\), and \(\lambda \ge -1\) be given by \autoref{lem:key-lemma}, applied with \begin{equation} \alpha_i = \frac{p_i(X,Y_i) - p_0 + \delta}{t} \end{equation} for each \(i \in [r]\), and go to Step~2.\smallskip \item Colour step: If \(\lambda \le \lambda_0\), then choose a colour \(j \in [r]\) such that the set \begin{equation*} X'' = N_j(x) \cap X' \end{equation*} has at least \((|X'| - 1)/r\) elements, and update the sets as follows: \begin{equation*} X \to X'', \qquad Y_j \to Y'_j \qquad \text{and} \qquad T_j \to T_j \cup \{x\} \end{equation*} and go to Step~1. Otherwise go to Step~3.\smallskip \item Density-boost step: If \(\lambda > \lambda_0\), then we update the sets as follows: \begin{equation*} X \to X' \qquad \text{and} \qquad Y_\ell \to Y'_\ell, \end{equation*} and go to Step~1. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Repeatedly apply the key lemma; take a colour step if $\lambda\le\lambda_0$, else a density-boost step, until some $T_i$ has size $t$ or $X$ is empty.
nodes.label: alg:book

nodes.name: Apply the key lemma
nodes.statement_short: Apply the key lemma with $\alpha_i=(p_i-p_0+\delta)/t$
nodes.label: Alg:Step1

nodes.name: Colour step
nodes.statement_short: If $\lambda\le\lambda_0$, add $x$ to $T_j$ for a popular colour $j$ and shrink $X$
nodes.label: Alg:Step2

nodes.name: Density-boost step
nodes.statement_short: If $\lambda>\lambda_0$, pass to $X'$ and $Y'_\ell$
nodes.label: Alg:Step3

nodes.name: Minimum initial density p_0
nodes.statement: Recall that we are given an \(r\)-colouring \(\chi\) of \(E(K_n)\) and sets \(X,Y_1,\ldots,Y_r \subset V(K_n)\), define \begin{equation} p_0 = \min\big\{ p_i(X,Y_i) : i \in [r] \big\}, \end{equation} and run the algorithm for some \(t \in \N\), \(\lambda_0 \ge -1\) and \(\delta > 0\).
nodes.statement_short: $p_0=\min_i p_i(X,Y_i)$ for the input sets; the algorithm is run with parameters $t,\lambda_0,\delta$.

nodes.name: Algorithm state notation X(s), Y_i(s), p_i(s), α_i(s)
nodes.statement: In order to simplify the statements of the lemmas below, let us write \(X(s)\) and \(Y_i(s)\) for the sets \(X\) and \(Y_i\) after \(s\) steps of the algorithm, and set \begin{equation*} p_i(s) = p_i\big( X(s), Y_i(s) \big) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \alpha_i(s) = \frac{p_i(s) - p_0 + \delta}{t}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Sets after $s$ steps, their densities $p_i(s)$, and the step sizes $\alpha_i(s)$.

nodes.name: Density-boost step sets B_i(s)
nodes.statement: Let us also write \(\ell(s) \in [r]\) and \(\lambda(s) \ge -1\) for the colour and number given by the application of \autoref{key:lemma} to the sets \(X(s)\) and \(Y_1(s),\dots,Y_r(s)\), and define \begin{equation*} \cB_i(s) = \big\{ 0 \le j < s \,:\, \ell(j) = i \, \text{ and } \, \lambda(j) > \lambda_0 \big\}, \end{equation*} for each \(i \in [r]\) and \(s \in \N\), to be the set of density-boost steps in colour \(i\) during the first \(s\) steps of the algorithm.
nodes.statement_short: $\ell(s),\lambda(s)$ from the key lemma at step $s$; $\mathcal B_i(s)$ the density-boost steps in colour $i$ before $s$.

nodes.name: Lower bound for p_i during algorithm
nodes.statement: \paperref{Lemma 4.1} For each \(i \in [r]\) and \(s \in \N\), \begin{equation} p_i(s) - p_0 + \delta \, \ge \, \delta \cdot \bigg( 1 - \frac{1}{t} \bigg)^{t} \prod_{j \in \cB_i(s)} \bigg( 1 + \frac{\lambda(j)}{t} \bigg). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $p_i(s)-p_0+\delta$ shrinks by at most $(1-1/t)^t$ overall and grows by $1+\lambda(j)/t$ at each boost step.
nodes.label: lem:pi:lower:bound

nodes.name: Proof of lower bound for p_i
nodes.statement: Note first that if \(Y_i(s+1) = Y_i(s)\), then \(p_i(s+1) \ge p_i(s)\), since the minimum degree does not decrease when we take a subset of \(X(s)\). When we perform a colour step in colour \(i\), we have \(p_i(s+1) \ge p_i(s) - \alpha_i(s)\), by \autoref{lem:key-lemma}, and hence \begin{equation*} p_i(s+1) - p_0 + \delta \ge \bigg( 1 - \frac{1}{t} \bigg) \big( p_i(s) - p_0 + \delta \big), \end{equation*} by our choice of \(\alpha_i(s)\). Similarly, when we perform a density-boost step in colour \(i\) we have \(p_i(s+1) \ge p_i(s) + \lambda(s) \alpha_i(s)\), by \autoref{lem:key-lemma}, and hence \begin{equation*} p_i(s+1) - p_0 + \delta \ge \bigg( 1 + \frac{\lambda(s)}{t} \bigg) \big( p_i(s) - p_0 + \delta \big). \end{equation*} Recalling that there are at most \(t\) colour steps in colour \(i\), and that \(p_i(0) \ge p_0\), by the definition~\eqref{def:p0} of \(p_0\), the claimed bound follows.
nodes.statement_short: Track $p_i(s)-p_0+\delta$ step by step: unchanged, $\times(1-1/t)$ at colour steps, $\times(1+\lambda/t)$ at boost steps.

nodes.name: Unchanged Y_i
nodes.statement: Note first that if \(Y_i(s+1) = Y_i(s)\), then \(p_i(s+1) \ge p_i(s)\), since the minimum degree does not decrease when we take a subset of \(X(s)\).
nodes.statement_short: Density does not drop when only $X$ shrinks

nodes.name: Colour step
nodes.statement: When we perform a colour step in colour \(i\), we have \(p_i(s+1) \ge p_i(s) - \alpha_i(s)\), by \autoref{lem:key-lemma}, and hence \begin{equation*} p_i(s+1) - p_0 + \delta \ge \bigg( 1 - \frac{1}{t} \bigg) \big( p_i(s) - p_0 + \delta \big), \end{equation*} by our choice of \(\alpha_i(s)\).
nodes.statement_short: Key lemma: factor $(1-1/t)$

nodes.name: Density-boost step
nodes.statement: Similarly, when we perform a density-boost step in colour \(i\) we have \(p_i(s+1) \ge p_i(s) + \lambda(s) \alpha_i(s)\), by \autoref{lem:key-lemma}, and hence \begin{equation*} p_i(s+1) - p_0 + \delta \ge \bigg( 1 + \frac{\lambda(s)}{t} \bigg) \big( p_i(s) - p_0 + \delta \big). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Key lemma: factor $(1+\lambda/t)$

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Recalling that there are at most \(t\) colour steps in colour \(i\), and that \(p_i(0) \ge p_0\), by the definition~\eqref{def:p0} of \(p_0\), the claimed bound follows.
nodes.statement_short: At most $t$ colour steps per colour

nodes.name: Minimum bound on p_i
nodes.statement: \paperref{Lemma 4.2} If \(t \ge 2\), then \begin{equation*} p_i(s) \, \ge \, p_0 - \frac{3\delta}{4} \end{equation*} for every \(i \in [r]\) and \(s \in \N\).
nodes.label: lem:pi:minp

nodes.name: Proof of minimum bound on p_i
nodes.statement: Bound follows immediately from~\eqref{eq:pi:lower:bound} and the definition of \(\alpha_i(s)\).
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the lower bound on $p_i(s)-p_0+\delta$.

nodes.name: Minimum bound on α_i
nodes.statement: \paperref{Lemma 4.2} If \(t \ge 2\), then \begin{equation*} \alpha_i(s) \, \ge \, \frac{\delta}{4t} \end{equation*} for every \(i \in [r]\) and \(s \in \N\).
nodes.label: lem:pi:mina

nodes.name: Proof of minimum bound on α_i
nodes.statement: Bound follows immediately from~\eqref{eq:pi:lower:bound} and the definition of \(\alpha_i(s)\).
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the lower bound on $p_i(s)-p_0+\delta$.

nodes.name: Upper bound on density-boost steps
nodes.statement: \paperref{Lemma 4.3} If \(t \ge \lambda_0\) and \(\delta \le 1/4\), then \begin{equation*} |\cB_i(s)| \le \frac{4 \log(1/\delta)}{\lambda_0} \cdot t \end{equation*} for every \(i \in [r]\) and \(s \in \N\).
nodes.label: lem:Bi:max

nodes.name: Proof of upper bound on density-boost steps
nodes.statement: Since \(\lambda(j) > \lambda_0\) for every \(j \in \cB_i(s)\), and \(p_i(s) \le 1\), it follows from~\eqref{eq:pi:lower:bound} that \begin{equation*} \frac{\delta}{4} \bigg( 1 + \frac{\lambda_0}{t} \bigg)^{|\cB_i(s)|} \le 1 + \delta. \end{equation*} Since \(t \ge \lambda_0\) and \(\delta \le 1/4\), the claimed bound follows.
nodes.statement_short: Each boost multiplies $p_i-p_0+\delta\le1+\delta$ by $1+\lambda_0/t$; take logs.

nodes.name: Lower bound for Y_i set sizes
nodes.statement: \paperref{Lemma 4.4} If \(t \ge 2\), then \begin{equation*} |Y_i(s)| \ge \bigg( p_0 - \frac{3\delta}{4} \bigg)^{t + |\cB_i(s)|} |Y_i(0)| \end{equation*} for every \(i \in [r]\) and \(s \in \N\).
nodes.label: lem:Y:lower:bound

nodes.name: Proof of lower bound for Y_i set sizes
nodes.statement: Note that \(Y_i(j+1) \ne Y_i(j)\) for at most \(t + |\cB_i(s)|\) of the first \(s\) steps, and for those steps we have \begin{equation*} |Y_i(j+1)| = p_i(j) |Y_i(j)| \ge \bigg( p_0 - \frac{3\delta}{4} \bigg) |Y_i(j)|, \end{equation*} by~\eqref{eq:key:alli} and \autoref{lem:pi:mina}.
nodes.statement_short: $Y_i$ changes in at most $t+|\mathcal B_i(s)|$ steps, each time shrinking by factor $p_i(j)\ge p_0-3\delta/4$.

nodes.name: ε and the set B(s) of density-boost steps
nodes.statement: To do so, set \(\eps = (\beta / r) e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda_0 + 1}}\), and define \(\cB(s) = \cB_1(s) \cup \cdots \cup \cB_r(s)\) to be the set of all density-boost steps.

nodes.name: Lower bound for reservoir X size
nodes.statement: \paperref{Lemma 4.5} For each \(s \in \N\), \begin{equation} |X(s)| \ge \eps^{rt + |\cB(s)|} \exp\bigg( - C \sum_{j \in \cB(s)} \sqrt{\lambda(j)+1}\,\, \bigg) |X(0)| - rt. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $|X(s)|$ loses a factor $\varepsilon$ per colour step and $\beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda+1}}$ per boost step.
nodes.label: lem:X:lower:bound

nodes.name: Proof of lower bound for reservoir X size
nodes.statement: If \(\lambda(j) \le \lambda_0\), then by~\eqref{eq:key:ell} and Step~2 of the algorithm we have \begin{equation*} |X(j+1)| \ge \frac{\beta e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda_0 + 1}}}{r} \cdot |X(j)| - 1 = \eps |X(j)| - 1. \end{equation*} On the other hand, if \(\lambda(j) > \lambda_0\), then \(j \in \cB(s)\), and we have \begin{equation*} |X(j+1)| \ge \beta e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda(j) + 1}} |X(j)|, \end{equation*} by~\eqref{eq:key:ell} and Step~3 of the algorithm. Since there are at most \(rt\) colour steps, and \(\beta \ge \eps\), the claimed bound follows.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the shrinkage of $X$ at colour steps and at density-boost steps via the key lemma, then multiply.

nodes.name: Colour step
nodes.statement: If \(\lambda(j) \le \lambda_0\), then by~\eqref{eq:key:ell} and Step~2 of the algorithm we have \begin{equation*} |X(j+1)| \ge \frac{\beta e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda_0 + 1}}}{r} \cdot |X(j)| - 1 = \eps |X(j)| - 1. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Shrink by factor $\varepsilon$ minus one

nodes.name: Density-boost step
nodes.statement: On the other hand, if \(\lambda(j) > \lambda_0\), then \(j \in \cB(s)\), and we have \begin{equation*} |X(j+1)| \ge \beta e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda(j) + 1}} |X(j)|, \end{equation*} by~\eqref{eq:key:ell} and Step~3 of the algorithm.
nodes.statement_short: Shrink by factor $\beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda(j)+1}}$

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since there are at most \(rt\) colour steps, and \(\beta \ge \eps\), the claimed bound follows.
nodes.statement_short: At most $rt$ colour steps

nodes.name: Sum of λ parameters bound
nodes.statement: \paperref{Lemma 4.6} If \(t \ge \lambda_0 / \delta > 0\) and \(\delta \le 1/4\), then \begin{equation*} \sum_{j \in \cB(s)} \sqrt{\lambda(j)} \le \frac{7r \log(1/\delta)}{\sqrt{\lambda_0}} \cdot t \end{equation*} for every \(s \in \N\).
nodes.label: lem:sum:of:lambdas

nodes.name: Proof of sum of λ parameters bound
nodes.statement: Observe first that, by \autoref{lem:pi:lower:bound}, we have \begin{equation} \frac{\delta}{4} \prod_{j \in \cB_i(s)} \bigg( 1 + \frac{\lambda(j)}{t} \bigg) \le 1 + \delta \end{equation} for each \(i \in [r]\). Note also that \(\lambda_0 \le \lambda(j) \le 5t/\delta\) for every \(j \in \cB(s)\), where the lower bound holds by the definition of \(\cB(s)\), and the upper bound by~\eqref{eq:B:condition} and since \(\delta \le 1/4\). Now, since \(\log(1+x) \ge \min\{ x/2,1\}\) for all \(x > 0\), it follows that \begin{equation} \frac{ \sqrt{\lambda(j)} }{\log(1 + \lambda(j)/t) } \le \max\bigg\{ \frac{ 2t }{ \sqrt{\lambda_0} }, \, \sqrt{ \frac{5t}{\delta}} \bigg\} \le \frac{ 3t }{ \sqrt{\lambda_0} }, \end{equation} where in the second inequality we used our assumption that \(t \ge \lambda_0 / \delta\). It now follows that \begin{equation*} \sum_{j \in \cB_i(s)} \sqrt{\lambda(j)} \le \frac{ 3t }{ \sqrt{\lambda_0} } \sum_{j \in \cB_i(s)} \log \bigg( 1 + \frac{\lambda(j)}{t} \bigg) \le \frac{7 \log(1/\delta)}{\sqrt{\lambda_0}} \cdot t, \end{equation*} where the first inequality holds by~\eqref{eq:not:convexity}, and the second follows from~\eqref{eq:B:condition}, since \(\delta \le 1/4\). Summing over \(i \in [r]\), we obtain the claimed bound.
nodes.statement_short: Compare $\sqrt{\lambda(j)}$ with $\log(1+\lambda(j)/t)$ and use the product bound from the $p_i$ lower bound.

nodes.name: Product bound
nodes.statement: Observe first that, by \autoref{lem:pi:lower:bound}, we have \begin{equation} \frac{\delta}{4} \prod_{j \in \cB_i(s)} \bigg( 1 + \frac{\lambda(j)}{t} \bigg) \le 1 + \delta \end{equation} for each \(i \in [r]\).
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound on $p_i$ bounds the boost product

nodes.name: Range of λ(j)
nodes.statement: Note also that \(\lambda_0 \le \lambda(j) \le 5t/\delta\) for every \(j \in \cB(s)\), where the lower bound holds by the definition of \(\cB(s)\), and the upper bound by~\eqref{eq:B:condition} and since \(\delta \le 1/4\).

nodes.statement_short: Sum over $\mathcal B_i(s)$

nodes.name: Book theorem
nodes.statement: \paperref{Theorem 2.1} Let \(\chi\) be an \(r\)-colouring of \(E(K_n)\), and let \(X,Y_1,\ldots,Y_r \subset V(K_n)\). For every \(p > 0\) and \(\mu \ge 2^{10} r^3\), and every \(t,m \in \N\) with \(t \ge \mu^5 / p\), the following holds. If \begin{equation*} |N_i(x) \cap Y_i| \ge p|Y_i| \end{equation*} for every \(x \in X\) and \(i \in [r]\), and moreover \begin{equation*} |X| \ge \bigg( \frac{\mu^2}{p} \bigg)^{\mu r t} \qquad \text{and} \qquad |Y_i| \ge \bigg( \frac{e^{2^{13} r^3 / \mu^2}}{p} \bigg)^t \, m, \end{equation*} then \(\chi\) contains a monochromatic \((t,m)\)-book.
assumptions: For every \(p > 0\) and \(\mu \ge 2^{10} r^3\), and every \(t,m \in \N\) with \(t \ge \mu^5 / p\)
\begin{equation*} |N_i(x) \cap Y_i| \ge p|Y_i| \end{equation*} for every \(x \in X\) and \(i \in [r]\)
nodes.statement_short: If every $x\in X$ has colour-$i$ density $\ge p$ into $Y_i$ and $X$, $Y_i$ are large enough, the colouring contains a monochromatic $(t,m)$-book.
nodes.label: thm:book

nodes.name: Proof of the book theorem
nodes.statement: Recall that we are given an \(r\)-colouring \(\chi\) of \(E(K_n)\) and a collection of sets \(X,Y_1,\ldots,Y_r \subset V(K_n)\) with \begin{equation} |X| \ge \bigg( \frac{\mu^2}{p} \bigg)^{\mu r t} \qquad \text{and} \qquad |Y_i| \ge \bigg( \frac{e^{2^{13} r^3 / \mu^2}}{p} \bigg)^t \, m \end{equation} for each \(i \in [r]\), for some \(p > 0\), \(\mu \ge 2^{10} r^3\) and \(t,m \in \N\) with \(t \ge \mu^5 / p\), and moreover \begin{equation} |N_i(x) \cap Y_i| \ge p|Y_i| \end{equation} for every \(x \in X\) and \(i \in [r]\). We will run the multicolour book algorithm with \begin{equation*} \delta = \frac{p}{\mu^2} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \lambda_0 = \bigg( \frac{\mu \log(1/\delta)}{8C} \bigg)^2, \end{equation*} where \(C = 4r^{3/2}\) (as before), and show that it ends with \begin{equation*} \max \big\{ |T_i(s)| : i \in [r] \big\} = t \qquad \text{and} \qquad \min\big\{ |Y_i(s)| : i \in [r] \big\} \ge m, \end{equation*} and therefore produces a monochromatic \((t,m)\)-book. To do so, we just need to bound the sizes of the sets \(X(s)\) and \(Y_i(s)\) from below. Observe that \(t \ge \lambda_0\) and \(\delta \le 1/4\), and therefore, by \autoref{lem:Bi:max}, that \begin{equation} |\cB_i(s)| \, \le \, \frac{4 \log(1/\delta)}{\lambda_0} \cdot t \, = \, \frac{2^{12} r^3}{\mu^2 \log(1/\delta)} \cdot t \, \le \, t \end{equation} for every \(i \in [r]\) and \(s \in \N\). Since \(p_0 \ge p\), by~\eqref{eq:book:thm:min:degree} and the definition of \(p_0\), it follows that \begin{equation*} |Y_i(s)| \, \ge \, \bigg( p - \frac{3\delta}{4} \bigg)^{t + |\cB_i(s)|} |Y_i| \, \ge \, e^{-2\delta t / p} \, p^{|\cB_i(s)|} \, \big( e^{2^{13} r^3 / \mu^2} \big)^t \, m, \end{equation*} where the first inequality holds by \autoref{lem:Y:lower:bound}, and the second by~\eqref{eq:book:thm:conditions} and~\eqref{eq:Bi:final:bound}. Noting that \(p^{|\cB_i(s)|} \ge e^{-2^{12} r^3 t / \mu^2}\), by~\eqref{eq:Bi:final:bound}, and that \(\delta / p = 1/\mu^2\), it follows that \begin{equation*} |Y_i(s)| \, \ge \, e^{-2 t / \mu^2} \big( e^{2^{12} r^3 / \mu^2} \big)^t \, m \, \ge \, m, \end{equation*} as claimed. To bound \(|X(s)|\), recall~\eqref{eq:X:lower:bound} and observe that \begin{equation*} \eps^{rt + |\cB(s)|} \ge \bigg( \frac{\beta}{r} \cdot e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda_0 + 1}} \bigg)^{2rt} \ge \big( e^{- 4C \sqrt{\lambda_0}} \big)^{rt} = \delta^{\mu r t/2} = \bigg( \frac{\mu^2}{p} \bigg)^{-\mu r t / 2}, \end{equation*} where the first step holds because \(\eps = (\beta / r) e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda_0 + 1}}\) and \(|\cB(s)| \le rt\), by~\eqref{eq:Bi:final:bound}, and the second step holds because \(\beta = 3^{-4r}\) and \(\lambda_0 \ge 2^{10} r^3\). Moreover, we have \begin{equation*} \sum_{j \in \cB(s)} \sqrt{\lambda(j)+1} \le \frac{8r \log(1/\delta)}{\sqrt{\lambda_0}} \cdot t = \frac{2^6Crt}{\mu}, \end{equation*} by \autoref{lem:sum:of:lambdas} and our choice of \(\lambda_0\), and therefore \begin{equation*} |X(s)| \ge \bigg( \frac{\mu^2}{p} \bigg)^{\mu r t / 2} \exp\bigg( - \frac{2^6C^2rt}{\mu} \bigg) - rt > 0, \end{equation*} for every \(s \in \N\), by \autoref{lem:X:lower:bound} and since \(\mu \ge 2^{10} r^3\) and \(C = 4r^{3/2}\). It follows that the algorithm produces a monochromatic \((t,m)\)-book, as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Run the multicolour book algorithm with $\delta=p/\mu^2$ and suitable $\lambda_0$; the lemmas keep $X(s)$ non-empty and $|Y_i(s)|\ge m$ until some $T_i$ reaches size $t$.

nodes.statement: Recall that we are given an \(r\)-colouring \(\chi\) of \(E(K_n)\) and a collection of sets \(X,Y_1,\ldots,Y_r \subset V(K_n)\) with \begin{equation} |X| \ge \bigg( \frac{\mu^2}{p} \bigg)^{\mu r t} \qquad \text{and} \qquad |Y_i| \ge \bigg( \frac{e^{2^{13} r^3 / \mu^2}}{p} \bigg)^t \, m \end{equation} for each \(i \in [r]\), for some \(p > 0\), \(\mu \ge 2^{10} r^3\) and \(t,m \in \N\) with \(t \ge \mu^5 / p\), and moreover \begin{equation} |N_i(x) \cap Y_i| \ge p|Y_i| \end{equation} for every \(x \in X\) and \(i \in [r]\).

nodes.statement: To do so, we just need to bound the sizes of the sets \(X(s)\) and \(Y_i(s)\) from below.

nodes.name: Bound Y_i(s)
nodes.statement: Since \(p_0 \ge p\), by~\eqref{eq:book:thm:min:degree} and the definition of \(p_0\), it follows that \begin{equation*} |Y_i(s)| \, \ge \, \bigg( p - \frac{3\delta}{4} \bigg)^{t + |\cB_i(s)|} |Y_i| \, \ge \, e^{-2\delta t / p} \, p^{|\cB_i(s)|} \, \big( e^{2^{13} r^3 / \mu^2} \big)^t \, m, \end{equation*} where the first inequality holds by \autoref{lem:Y:lower:bound}, and the second by~\eqref{eq:book:thm:conditions} and~\eqref{eq:Bi:final:bound}.

nodes.name: Y_i(s) ≥ m
nodes.statement: Noting that \(p^{|\cB_i(s)|} \ge e^{-2^{12} r^3 t / \mu^2}\), by~\eqref{eq:Bi:final:bound}, and that \(\delta / p = 1/\mu^2\), it follows that \begin{equation*} |Y_i(s)| \, \ge \, e^{-2 t / \mu^2} \big( e^{2^{12} r^3 / \mu^2} \big)^t \, m \, \ge \, m, \end{equation*} as claimed.

nodes.statement: To bound \(|X(s)|\), recall~\eqref{eq:X:lower:bound} and observe that \begin{equation*} \eps^{rt + |\cB(s)|} \ge \bigg( \frac{\beta}{r} \cdot e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda_0 + 1}} \bigg)^{2rt} \ge \big( e^{- 4C \sqrt{\lambda_0}} \big)^{rt} = \delta^{\mu r t/2} = \bigg( \frac{\mu^2}{p} \bigg)^{-\mu r t / 2}, \end{equation*} where the first step holds because \(\eps = (\beta / r) e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda_0 + 1}}\) and \(|\cB(s)| \le rt\), by~\eqref{eq:Bi:final:bound}, and the second step holds because \(\beta = 3^{-4r}\) and \(\lambda_0 \ge 2^{10} r^3\).

nodes.name: X(s) > 0
nodes.statement: Moreover, we have \begin{equation*} \sum_{j \in \cB(s)} \sqrt{\lambda(j)+1} \le \frac{8r \log(1/\delta)}{\sqrt{\lambda_0}} \cdot t = \frac{2^6Crt}{\mu}, \end{equation*} by \autoref{lem:sum:of:lambdas} and our choice of \(\lambda_0\), and therefore \begin{equation*} |X(s)| \ge \bigg( \frac{\mu^2}{p} \bigg)^{\mu r t / 2} \exp\bigg( - \frac{2^6C^2rt}{\mu} \bigg) - rt > 0, \end{equation*} for every \(s \in \N\), by \autoref{lem:X:lower:bound} and since \(\mu \ge 2^{10} r^3\) and \(C = 4r^{3/2}\).

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: It follows that the algorithm produces a monochromatic \((t,m)\)-book, as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: The algorithm outputs a book

nodes.name: Deduction of the main theorem
nodes.statement: In this section we will deduce \autoref{thm:Ramsey:multicolour}, the bound on the Ramsey numbers \(R_r(k)\), from \autoref{thm:book}. We will in fact prove a stronger quantitative version of the theorem in the form of \autoref{thm:Ramsey:multicolour:quant}.
nodes.section: 6 Deducing the Bound on the Ramsey Number
nodes.statement_short: The main theorem is deduced from the book theorem via its quantitative version.

nodes.name: Single Erdős-Szekeres step
nodes.statement: \paperref{Lemma 5.2} Given \(n,r \in \N\) and \(\eps > 0\), and an \(r\)-colouring of \(E(K_n)\), the following holds. There exist disjoint sets of vertices \(S_1,\dots,S_r\) and \(W\) such that, for every \(i \in [r]\), \begin{equation*} |W| \ge \bigg( \frac{1+\eps}{r} \bigg)^{\sum_{j = 1}^r |S_j|} n \qquad \text{and} \qquad |N_i(w) \cap W| \ge \bigg( \frac{1}{r} - \eps \bigg) |W| - 1 \end{equation*} for every \(w \in W\), and \((S_i,W)\) is a monochromatic book in colour~\(i\).
nodes.section: 6 Deducing the Bound on the Ramsey Number
conclusions: There exist disjoint sets of vertices \(S_1,\dots,S_r\) and \(W\) such that, for every \(i \in [r]\), \begin{equation*} |W| \ge \bigg( \frac{1+\eps}{r} \bigg)^{\sum_{j = 1}^r |S_j|} n \qquad \text{and} \qquad |N_i(w) \cap W| \ge \bigg( \frac{1}{r} - \eps \bigg) |W| - 1 \end{equation*} for every \(w \in W\), and \((S_i,W)\) is a monochromatic book in colour~\(i\).
nodes.statement_short: The Erdős–Szekeres process yields books $(S_i,W)$ with $W$ large and nearly $1/r$-regular in each colour.
nodes.label: lem:ESz:steps

nodes.name: Proof of single Erdős-Szekeres step
nodes.statement: We use induction on~\(n\). Note that if \(n \le r\) or \(r = 1\), then the sets \(S_1 = \cdots = S_r = \emptyset\) and \(W = V(K_n)\) have the required properties. We may therefore assume that \(n > r \ge 2\), and that there exists a vertex \(x \in V(K_n)\) and a colour \(\ell \in [r]\) such that \begin{equation*} |N_\ell(x)| < \bigg( \frac{1}{r} - \eps \bigg) n - 1, \end{equation*} and hence there exists a different colour \(j \ne \ell\) such that \begin{equation*} |N_j(x)| \ge \frac{1}{r-1} \bigg( n - \bigg( \frac{1}{r} - \eps \bigg) n \bigg) \ge \bigg( \frac{1 + \eps}{r} \bigg) n. \end{equation*} Applying the induction hypothesis to the colouring induced by the set \(N_j(x)\), we obtain sets \(S'_1,\ldots,S'_r\) and \(W'\) satisfying the conclusion of the lemma with \(n\) replaced by \(|N_j(x)|\). Setting \begin{equation*} W = W', \qquad S_j = S'_j \cup \{x\} \qquad \text{and} \qquad S_i = S'_i \qquad \text{for each } \, i \ne j, \end{equation*} we see that \(W\) satisfies the minimum degree condition (by the induction hypothesis), and \begin{equation*} |W| \ge \bigg( \frac{1+\eps}{r} \bigg)^{\sum_{i = 1}^r |S'_i|}|N_j(x)| \ge \bigg( \frac{1+\eps}{r} \bigg)^{\sum_{i=1}^r |S_i|}n. \end{equation*} Since \((S_i,W)\) is a monochromatic book in colour~\(i\) for each \(i \in [r]\), it follows that \(S_1,\dots,S_r\) and \(W\) are sets with the claimed properties.
nodes.section: 6 Deducing the Bound on the Ramsey Number
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$: a vertex of low degree in some colour has high degree in another; recurse into that neighbourhood.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: We use induction on~\(n\). Note that if \(n \le r\) or \(r = 1\), then the sets \(S_1 = \cdots = S_r = \emptyset\) and \(W = V(K_n)\) have the required properties.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$; trivial sets for $n\le r$ or $r=1$
nodes.section: 6 Deducing the Bound on the Ramsey Number

nodes.name: High-degree colour
nodes.statement: We may therefore assume that \(n > r \ge 2\), and that there exists a vertex \(x \in V(K_n)\) and a colour \(\ell \in [r]\) such that \begin{equation*} |N_\ell(x)| < \bigg( \frac{1}{r} - \eps \bigg) n - 1, \end{equation*} and hence there exists a different colour \(j \ne \ell\) such that \begin{equation*} |N_j(x)| \ge \frac{1}{r-1} \bigg( n - \bigg( \frac{1}{r} - \eps \bigg) n \bigg) \ge \bigg( \frac{1 + \eps}{r} \bigg) n. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: A low-degree vertex in colour $\ell$ has large degree in some $j$
nodes.section: 6 Deducing the Bound on the Ramsey Number

nodes.name: Apply hypothesis
nodes.statement: Applying the induction hypothesis to the colouring induced by the set \(N_j(x)\), we obtain sets \(S'_1,\ldots,S'_r\) and \(W'\) satisfying the conclusion of the lemma with \(n\) replaced by \(|N_j(x)|\).
nodes.statement_short: Recurse into $N_j(x)$
nodes.section: 6 Deducing the Bound on the Ramsey Number

nodes.name: Extend books
nodes.statement: Setting \begin{equation*} W = W', \qquad S_j = S'_j \cup \{x\} \qquad \text{and} \qquad S_i = S'_i \qquad \text{for each } \, i \ne j, \end{equation*} we see that \(W\) satisfies the minimum degree condition (by the induction hypothesis), and \begin{equation*} |W| \ge \bigg( \frac{1+\eps}{r} \bigg)^{\sum_{i = 1}^r |S'_i|}|N_j(x)| \ge \bigg( \frac{1+\eps}{r} \bigg)^{\sum_{i=1}^r |S_i|}n. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Add $x$ to $S_j$ and check size of $W$
nodes.section: 6 Deducing the Bound on the Ramsey Number

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since \((S_i,W)\) is a monochromatic book in colour~\(i\) for each \(i \in [r]\), it follows that \(S_1,\dots,S_r\) and \(W\) are sets with the claimed properties.
nodes.statement_short: Sets have the claimed properties

nodes.name: Many Erdős-Szekeres steps bound
nodes.statement: \paperref{Lemma 5.3} Let \(k,r \ge 2\) and \(\eps \in (0,1)\). We have \begin{equation*} R_r\big( k - s_1, \ldots, k - s_r \big) \le e^{-\eps^3 k / 2} \bigg( \frac{1+\eps}{r} \bigg)^s r^{rk} \end{equation*} for every \(s_1,\ldots,s_r \in [k]\) with \(s = s_1 + \cdots + s_r \ge \eps^2 k\).
nodes.section: 6 Deducing the Bound on the Ramsey Number
assumptions: for every \(s_1,\ldots,s_r \in [k]\) with \(s = s_1 + \cdots + s_r \ge \eps^2 k\)
conclusions: \begin{equation*} R_r\big( k - s_1, \ldots, k - s_r \big) \le e^{-\eps^3 k / 2} \bigg( \frac{1+\eps}{r} \bigg)^s r^{rk} \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:many:ESz:steps

nodes.name: Proof of many Erdős-Szekeres steps bound
nodes.statement: By the Erd\H{o}s--Szekeres bound, we have \begin{equation*} R_r\big( k - s_1, \ldots, k - s_r \big) \le r^{rk - s}. \end{equation*} The claimed bound follows, since \(( 1 + \eps )^{\eps^2 k} \ge e^{\eps^3 k/2}\) for every \(\eps \in (0,1)\).
nodes.section: 6 Deducing the Bound on the Ramsey Number
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Erdős–Szekeres bound and $(1+\varepsilon)^{\varepsilon^2k}\ge e^{\varepsilon^3k/2}$.

nodes.name: Quantitative main theorem
nodes.statement: \paperref{Theorem 5.1} Let \(r \ge 2\), and set \(\delta = 2^{-160} r^{-12}\). Then \begin{equation*} R_r(k) \le e^{-\delta k} r^{rk} \end{equation*} for every \(k \in \N\) with \(k \ge 2^{160} r^{16}\).
nodes.section: 6 Deducing the Bound on the Ramsey Number
nodes.statement_short: $R_r(k)\le e^{-\delta k}r^{rk}$ with $\delta=2^{-160}r^{-12}$ for $k\ge2^{160}r^{16}$.
nodes.label: thm:Ramsey:multicolour:quant

nodes.name: Proof of the quantitative main theorem
nodes.statement: Given \(r \ge 2\), set \(\delta = 2^{-160} r^{-12}\), let \(k \ge 2^{160} r^{16}\) and \(n \ge e^{-\delta k} r^{rk}\), and let \(\chi\) be an arbitrary \(r\)-colouring of \(E(K_n)\). Set \(\eps = 2^{-50} r^{-4}\), and let \(S_1,\ldots,S_r\) and \(W\) be the sets given by \autoref{lem:ESz:steps}. Suppose first that \(|S_1| + \cdots + |S_r| \ge \eps^2 k\), and observe that, by \autoref{lem:many:ESz:steps} and our lower bounds on \(n\) and \(|W|\), we have \begin{equation*} |W| \ge \bigg( \frac{1+\eps}{r} \bigg)^{\sum_{j = 1}^r |S_j|} e^{-\delta k} r^{rk} \ge R_r\big( k - |S_1|, \ldots, k - |S_r| \big). \end{equation*} Since \((S_i,W)\) is a monochromatic book in colour~\(i\) for each \(i \in [r]\), it follows that there exists a monochromatic copy of \(K_k\) in \(\chi\), as required. We may therefore assume from now on that \(|S_1| + \cdots + |S_r| \le \eps^2 k\). In this case we set \(X = Y_1 = \cdots = Y_r = W\), and apply \autoref{thm:book} to the colouring restricted to \(W\) with \begin{equation*} p = \frac{1}{r} - 2\eps, \qquad \mu = 2^{30} r^3, \qquad t = 2^{-40} r^{-3} k \qquad \text{and} \qquad m = R\big( k, \ldots, k, k - t \big). \end{equation*} In order to apply \autoref{thm:book}, we need to check that \(t \ge \mu^5/p\), and that \begin{equation*} |X| \ge \bigg( \frac{\mu^2}{p} \bigg)^{\mu r t} \qquad \text{and} \qquad |Y_i| \ge \bigg( \frac{e^{2^{13} r^3 / \mu^2}}{p} \bigg)^t \, m. \end{equation*} The first two of these inequalities are both easy: the first holds because \(k \ge 2^{160} r^{16}\), and for the second note that since \(n \ge r^{rk/2}\) and \(\sum_{j = 1}^r |S_j| \le rk/4\), we have \begin{equation*} |X| \ge \bigg( \frac{1+\eps}{r} \bigg)^{rk/4} r^{rk/2} \ge r^{rk/4} \ge \big( 2^{61} r^7 \big)^{2^{-10} r k} \ge \bigg( \frac{\mu^2}{p} \bigg)^{\mu r t}, \end{equation*} as required.
